The Nigerian Correctional Service has called on governments, private organisations, religious institutions and communities to support the reintegration of ex-offenders into society, warning that unemployment, economic hardship and stigmatisation could undermine their rehabilitation and push them back into crime. The Controller-General of Corrections, Sylvester Nwakuche, made the appeal during the presentation of 2026 aftercare vocational starter packs to discharged inmates in Abuja. He said sustained support was necessary to help them establish businesses and become productive members of society. Nwakuche said the service had provided starter packs to nearly 33 ex-offenders to enable them to put the vocational skills acquired during incarceration into practice. According to him, the aftercare programme is designed to bridge the gap between rehabilitation in correctional facilities and successful reintegration into society. “For many inmates, the journey back into society is often confronted by stigma, unemployment, economic hardship, and rejection. Without adequate support, these challenges may undermine the gains of rehabilitation and increase the risk of reoffending,” he said. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources The Controller-General explained that the starter packs covered seven vocational areas, including laundry, barbing, tailoring and fashion design, hairdressing, carpentry, masonry, and welding and metal fabrication. He said the trades were selected to provide the beneficiaries with opportunities for self-employment, entrepreneurship and economic independence. “These starter packs represent much more than tools of trade. They are instruments of empowerment, they are symbols of renewed confidence, and seeds of economic independence. “They represent our belief that today’s offenders can become tomorrow’s entrepreneurs, employers of labour, and responsible contributors to national development,” he added. The NCoS boss said empowering discharged inmates was also an investment in public safety, noting that successful reintegration would help reduce recidivism and build safer communities. He also called on employers and other stakeholders to look beyond the past mistakes of ex-offenders and give them opportunities to rebuild their lives. “Governments, private organisations, religious institutions, community leaders, families, and individuals must all play their part in dismantling the walls of stigma and creating an environment where reformed persons can strive,” he said. Earlier, the Director of Health and Welfare, Abdullahi Aldo, said the aftercare programme was designed to ensure that discharged inmates were not abandoned after regaining their freedom. He said the initiative provided starter packs, skills support and mentorship to help beneficiaries reintegrate into their families and communities. “The aftercare programme is designed to ensure that no ex-offender is abandoned at the gate of freedom,” Aldo said. He urged the beneficiaries to use the materials as a foundation for a new life and become responsible members of their communities. “Be good ambassadors of the service in your communities, and prove to the world that change is possible,” he said. This is not the first time the service has empowered ex-offenders. In November 2025, it gave starter packs to 24 inmates to help them become financially independent after their release.
